kill_argument: The revision explains why the authors' two published runs cannot be compared, but the explanation rests on a false statement about the authors' code, and the abstract still uses those runs as its one outside calibration. Sec. 2 says the public 401K.R 'does not fix the splits it draws on parallel workers'. In fact the script makes a 12-worker cluster and never registers it. foreach therefore runs sequentially, with the warning suppressed, and set.seed(1211) fixes the splits for given package versions. If the earlier run used the same script and seed, its jointly small gaps may come from shared splits. Then they say nothing about how wide a split-noise tolerance is, yet the abstract and conclusion infer from them that the tolerances are 'if anything, wide'. The error is mine (paper-r2 F10). What held: macros and typed literals; MDS80 at every pass; the forest and lasso caveats; the 7-of-10 cell comparison; the F9 fixes; the replication facts; validate and --strict; and a scratch compile (20 pp, clean) that matches the committed PDF.

findings.text: Selective use of the authors' second run. Section 2 ('Two runs by the same authors') and claim c-aerpp-rerun report only the closest cell of the AER P&P 2017 run (forest 5-fold, $9,252, 'within $5'). sources/notes.md (section 2, item 6 of section 3, and the section 5 table) records all ten cells: gaps of $5-33 at 5-fold and up to $154 at 2-fold (nnet 9,104 vs 8,950), all inside the pre-registered tolerances. This is the most relevant evidence the paper has for its task ('compare ... and explain any difference'). (a) It is an out-of-sample check that the tolerances are not too tight. (b) It calibrates the replication's differences: our largest testable gap (+$157, nnet 2-fold) is the size of the authors' own run-to-run gap. (c) The earlier run's lasso 5-fold SE (1,581 vs 2018's 1,558) suggests that the large published lasso spread recurs across the authors' runs. That bears directly on the lasso spread discrepancy the paper says it cannot explain. Whether the earlier run's parenthesised SE is the adjusted one must be checked. Quoting only the $5 cell overstates the stability of the authors' procedure. The paragraph also cites the 2018 journal article for the arXiv v4 contents and does not say that v4 and the AER P&P preprint carry the same earlier numbers (sources/hdm_penalty.md section 5).

findings.text: The abstract says the replicated lasso estimates 'vary several times less across splits than the published ones'. The published split estimates are not observed. Their spread is inferred from the two SE rows through the 1.4826 x (adj^2 - med^2)^{1/2} approximation. On our own lasso runs that approximation overstates the measured spread: the implied MAD is 295 against a measured MAD of 239 at K = 2. The body is careful ('the published SEs imply'); the abstract is not. Separately, Limitations says 'the familywise rate treats the ten cells as independent'. The Bonferroni bound needs no independence; only the combined 33% false-failure figure treats the cells as independent (decision_rules.H2_size_under_measured_ports).

findings.text: The authors' earlier run is read as a draw of run-to-run split noise, and two inferences are drawn from it that the evidence does not support. (a) Results, lasso paragraph: 'The large published lasso adjusted SEs recur in the authors' earlier run (1,785 and 1,581). This suggests that the wide lasso spread is a feature of the authors' procedure rather than of one run of it.' If the two runs used independent splits, the published-implied lasso split SD ($1,656 at K=2, $1,278 at K=5; S = 100) gives a run-to-run SD of the median of about $293 and $227. The observed lasso gaps are -$10 and +$15 (|z| 0.03 and 0.07). The chance that both are this small is about 0.001. Over all ten cells, sum z^2 = 2.95 on 10 df (p about 0.02). Under the replication's own observed spreads it is 5.8 (p about 0.17). So, on independent splits, the earlier run is evidence that the authors' realised lasso spread is narrow, which is what our runs show. That is the opposite of the sentence. If the runs instead shared splits, the recurring adjusted SE is mechanical and says nothing about 'procedure rather than one run'. Either way the sentence fails. Whether the splits were shared cannot be established. The public repository's history starts on 2017-06-01, after the earlier run (arXiv v4, 30 Dec 2016), so that run's code is not public. The public 401K.R calls set.seed(1211) and then draws splits inside foreach %dopar% on a makeCluster PSOCK cluster, with no clusterSetRNGStream or doRNG. So even the public code does not fix the worker splits. (b) Results yardstick paragraph: 'So the tolerances are not narrower than the authors' own run-to-run variation' and 'differences of the size we find also arise between two runs of the original code'. The 2016 code is not known to be the original code. The ten gaps are jointly smaller than the tolerance model predicts, so as a calibration they show the tolerances are, if anything, wide (consistent with 1.4826 being an upper bound). They do not show that the tolerances are adequate. (c) Abstract, yardstick paragraph and conclusion compare maxima ('our largest testable difference is of that size'; '+$157 is close to the authors' +$154'). That is the single cell where the two coincide, the same selective use paper-r1 F1 objected to in the other direction. Cell by cell, our absolute difference is larger in 7 of 10 cells (forest 5-fold $206 vs $5; boosting 5-fold $90 vs $21; nnet 5-fold $88 vs $27; tree 5-fold $63 vs $23). The RMS over the ten cells is about $99 for ours against $61 for theirs. 'Our differences are of the same order' holds only as an order of magnitude. Some of this is expected from our smaller S for forest and boosting and from the port deviations. In part this finding corrects my own paper-r1 F1 ruling, which invited reading the earlier run as an 'out-of-sample check that the tolerances are not too tight'.

findings.text: False statement about the authors' public code, which originates in my own paper-r2 F10 text. Sec. 2 says 'the review of this paper found that even the public script does not fix the splits it draws on parallel workers'. That is wrong for the script as published. 401K.R (identical at a8ef8ef and at the current head ff35d21) loads doParallel (line 36), sets options(warn=-1) (line 51) and set.seed(1211) (line 52), and creates cl <- makeCluster(12) (line 53). It never calls registerDoParallel(cl) or any other register function: a grep of 401K.R, ML_Functions.R and Moment_Functions.R for 'regist' finds nothing. With no registered backend, foreach's %dopar% (line 105) runs sequentially in the main R session, and the 'no parallel backend registered' warning is suppressed by warn = -1. The splits are drawn by runif(nrow(data)) inside DoubleML (Moment_Functions.R line 53) in that session, so set.seed(1211) does fix them for a given R and package set. The learners draw from the same stream, so the splits after the first also depend on the package versions. My round-2 reading assumed that the cluster was registered. In addition, 'The authors' public repository begins on 1 June 2017' is slightly off. The first commit (91e7d6c, 'start', adds Readme.Rmd) is dated 2017-05-31T18:06:49Z. The code arrives in a8ef8ef on 2017-06-01T00:54:16Z. Neither fact has a claim in claims.jsonl: the sentence cites 'the review of this paper', which is not a source. The error matters beyond one clause. As committed, the public script is seeded. If the earlier run used the same script and seed, the two runs may share part of their split stream. That would explain why the ten gaps are jointly smaller than independent split noise predicts (paper-r2 F10: sum z^2 = 2.95 on 10 df). It also bears on how the abstract and conclusion use those gaps (F12).

Whether the earlier run used this script and seed is not known.' Either way, write 'the code was first committed on 1 June 2017 (UTC)' or 'the repository was created on 31 May 2017', with a claim.

findings.text: The abstract (lines 58-60) and the conclusion (lines 944-945) read the authors' two published runs as calibrating the tolerances: they 'differ by $5 to $154 per cell, all inside our tolerances, which suggests that the tolerances are, if anything, wide'. Sec. 2 says that these gaps 'cannot be read as run-to-run split noise of one fixed procedure'. Sec. 6 says they 'are not a measure of the run-to-run variation of the original code'. The tolerances are split-noise tolerances. Gaps between runs that may share splits (F11) or differ in code say nothing about whether a split-noise tolerance is wide. The inference holds only under independent splits, which the paper itself disclaims. The paper has its own, better evidence for 'wide': tol_obs < tolerance in every cell (Table 5), and the observed split spread is narrower than the published-implied spread for every learner (Figure 3). The abstract and conclusion pick the weakest evidence for the point, and only the earlier run appears there. That is the reading my paper-r1 F1 ruling invited and paper-r2 F10 partly corrected.

Or attach 'if anything, wide' to the paper's own diagnostic (the descriptive tolerance from our split spread is smaller in every cell), which already has macros. Sec. 6 may keep its sentence if it adds 'if the splits were independent'.

findings.text: The replication counts are stated loosely. Limitations says 'replication.json records all 16 logged runs reproduced at the protocol tolerance'. The AI-use statement says the same and then adds that one run 'has no metrics to compare'. replication.json has 15 runs with status 'match' and timing-synthetic with status 'ran'. So 15 runs were compared and matched, and one was re-executed without comparison. The Limitations sentence omits the qualifier, and the AI-use sentence contradicts itself. The source of the wording is REPLICATION.md ('16 of 16 runs reproduced'). The Replicator's file is outside the paper, but the paper should not copy the overstatement. Nothing in the paper depends on timing-synthetic beyond the design's choice of S, so the substance is unaffected.
